utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'm sorry for the delay. That's because of the overtime of the previous case which was using this courtroom, which also shows that how punctuality is important to all those trials. Mr. Usher, will you please bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Please understand that you are under solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Sir Martin.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Before we finish with a few additional documents, I'd like to go back and follow up on a few things from yesterday. I'd like to direct your attention, please, to around the 19th of September, 1993. Did you meet on that day or about that time an ABiH officer by the name of Esad Humo?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I'd previously had a meeting with Arif Pasalic and then I had a separate meeting in his headquarters with Esad Humo, who is the deputy commander of one brigade of the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you recall whether Humo told you that day about a particular incident that had happened sometime previous to that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was -- he had two main things which were concerning him considerably. First of all, he said that he wanted to draw my attention to the fact that the HVO were using prisoners to dig trenches on the front lines. And secondly, he then said that, two days previously, four prisoners had been dressed up in HVO uniform and placed in front of the front lines. The object, of course, would be to draw fire, to see where the fire was coming from. One was seriously injured, but the other three managed to get back across the lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. It has come to my attention, and I apologise for not standing and making this objection sooner, but apparently Mr. Humo is deceased, is no longer within the jurisdiction of this Tribunal to bring him here to cross-examine him concerning the statements that Sir Martin Garrod is now making and they are introduced -- offered for the proof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It seems to me that we have come across this problem yesterday, and this Trial Chamber has made a ruling already. You may proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I perhaps add that Pasalic is certainly dead, he drowned, but to the best of my knowledge, Esad Humo is still alive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you discussed a bit the detention camps and specifically some visit that you had to the Dretelj camp. Let me ask you generally, during your various conversations with senior HVO officials, was any justification ever made to you or given to you as for the existence of these camps?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The camps tended to be a non-subject, and they were never really -- they never provided any justification for them, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. If I could ask you to look next at -- I think the binder's still there. If you can turn your attention to Exhibit 611.1. Again, we've worked our way toward the back of the binder. If you should come across it in a different -- if it might assist you or anyone else, it is a daily summary for the 24th of September, 1993, from CC Mostar to RC Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. If you would just -- I'm not going to ask you detailed questions about the first topic at all, but if you just cast your eyes down the first two pages, actually continuing over to the third page, but there's a substantial part of this report simply records a fairly extensive meeting or conversation you had with Slobodan Praljak on the -- about this date, the 24th of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And as you indicate in the first paragraph under number 2, "Political activity," was that -- was he in fact at that time, as of that time, the overall chief, I guess number one position, in other words, of the HVO army?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can direct you to the top of page 3. Primarily just for the Chamber's benefit, to tie into other evidence. As part of this conversation and meeting with General Praljak that day, were you seeking the HVO's permission for a BBC news team to come into Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I left it to the end of the discussion because I guessed it would be a contentious point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, please.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: And when I raised the subject -- he had been very cheerful and smiling up to then. He then became extremely angry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is this -- I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is this the same news team that Jeremy Bowen, to your knowledge, was part of?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Go ahead, please. I --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: He then gave a long tirade against the lack of impartiality of the BBC and said that he was not going to let the BBC into East Mostar under any circumstances. I then went back to the BBC and advised them to contact Slobodan Bozic and Bruno Stojic direct, which they did, and then they obtained agreement. So Praljak, to an extent, shall we say, was overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. Further down that page in another section toward the bottom, the paragraph above item 3, "Military activity," so it's the preceding paragraph, there are several references to a Colonel Akrap, A-K-R-A-P. Do you recall having any dealings with this man, either by telephone or in person or of any sort?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We met for the one and only time when I attended a meeting chaired by Mr. Tadic, who was leading on humanitarian affairs for the Croats, trying to arrange a joint Croat-Bosnian convoy, food convoy, up into Central Bosnia. And he was extremely disruptive and in fact virtually brought the whole meeting to a close by trying to swing the whole meeting on to the subject of casualty evacuation helicopters which, of course, was not the subject of the meeting at all. When I asked him what his job was, what his appointment was, he replied, "That is a secret."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you ever learn or were you ever made aware that this Colonel Akrap was an HV officer?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you to look at the top of the next page, and I will not ask you to cover the topic again, but is this simply a record of one of your conversations about moving approximately 500 detainees from Dretelj to the Croatian island of Korcula?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. That was Claudio Baranzani, the head of the ICRC, informed me of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: A name that may not have come up in your testimony as much as it might have, and I may have skipped over a few points yesterday, but just in case, in this report you also mention a man named Bogo -- I'm sorry, Bozo Raguz. Just for the record and in case he should come up in the future, can you tell us who he was and what his role was vis-a-vis you?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I met him when we got into Mostar because he was the liaison officer with the international communities for the HVO in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And was he, therefore, someone that you had some number of dealings with?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I met him on several occasions, yes, a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I ask you now to go to the next exhibit which hopefully should -- if you again just leaf down through the B/C/S translation, you should come to Exhibit 642.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you just confirm, please, this is a report, a daily summary from CC Mostar for the 13th of October, 1993, and directing your attention to the fourth page of the report. Are you familiar with the preparer of this report?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's Jesus Amatriain of the Spanish who I handed over to HCC Mostar when I moved to Zenica. He stayed in that position for a few weeks until I sent Philip Watkins down to take over the post.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, up on that last page above that under 6, there's a reference to an invitation by General Andabak and then some -- also a reference to Tuta and it says, "He and Tuta are the war lords of this area. Sir Martin Garrod knows Tuta and his story." Now, can you provide some light in terms of had you discussed with Mr. Amatriain or how is it that -- if you can give us some additional assistance when he says you know Tuta and his story, what was that based on?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for a start, I'm pretty certain that Jesus Amatriain was also present at the lunch that I had in the mayor of Siroki Brijeg's house. I'm sure he was. And so I knew that he had contacts with Ivan Andabak, because particularly with the Spanish link, and so no doubt we would have discussed these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On the prior page, there are -- he makes a report -- when I say he, Mr. Amatriain, makes the report that apparently concerning two Muslim villages that, according to this document, perhaps Mr. Tuta and Mr. Andabak had given some protection to, is one of the words that was used. Can you add anything to what's in this document about that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't. Of course, I was pleased to see that. The villages are fairly close to Mostar, south-west of Mostar, but I'm afraid I cannot really add anything to that. I did not know those two villages myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask you then please to go to Exhibit 643. Really, primarily, sir, I want -- if you can confirm again that this is a CC daily summary for Mostar for the 13th of October, 1993, also prepared by Jesus Amatriain.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Concerning I guess two quick items: On the second page under the heading B, "Minorities," toward the end of the paragraph titled "Comment," if you see that.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There's a reference to -- it says, "We did have not any problem yesterday due to the fact that General Andabak, Ivan, one of the HVO SF commander passed at that moment and ordered the MP to let us pass." A couple of questions. In common parlance, what would the MP be reference to?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he's referring to military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you ever hear any discussion or did Mr. Amatriain ever tell you anything about the authority of Mr. Andabak in connection with giving orders to the military police?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but that wouldn't surprise me, bearing in mind his seniority in the hierarchy of the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And next I'm going to direct your attention to a short paragraph a little below the middle of the page, where again it says, "HCC tried this afternoon to deal with the affair of providing school and water for people from Kozice, but Mr. Naletilic, M, nickname Tuta, was not available." I simply ask you again did Mr. Amatriain share any more information with you about his involvement if any with Tuta in that regard?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't recall any further information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I think the final question on this document, under item 6, does that, as far as you know, record a meeting that Mr. Amatriain did in fact have as indicated earlier, a meeting with Andabak that previous evening?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He said he was going to meet him and here he clearly did meet him the previous night. So it is clearly a record of his -- the discussions that they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I can ask you to go then to -- back to your end of tour report, which was a couple of documents, one or two documents down. We'll skip over a couple of documents, but it's --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Sir Martin, on this document I had promised to counsel yesterday that we would get back --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: May we have an exhibit number on that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course. 770.1. It's the end of tour report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir Martin, I indicated to the counsel and Chamber yesterday that I would take you back to the one question -- clarification, and it's on page 3, top of page 3, about the HV presence in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And about two-thirds of the way through that first paragraph, what would be the carry-over of paragraph 15, are the words "We were also aware of a build-up of HVO/HV in the Buna area south of Mostar."

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think that I put the question to you yesterday, I used the word, if you had observed or your teams this observed. Can you clarify please, if you can, the nature or basis of the awareness that you or your organisation had of that presence of HV troops in that location? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would almost certainly have come from the team M3, mike 3 based in Medjugorje, based on his sightings, but I cannot be categoric about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. In closing, Sir Martin, a couple of questions. After -- sometime soon after the ICTY had returned indictments against the men Dario Kordic and Tihomir Blaskic in approximately November 1995, did you have any conversations with any senior HVO officials about that indictment?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the objection is that this is well outside the scope of the indictment, and I believe this Honourable Trial Chamber yesterday indicated that we would not be dealing with the years of 1995 and 1996, and those years, and this is exactly where we're coming back full circle to 1996 now -- or 1995. It's inappropriate, it's outside the scope, and we object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, you have to show to us the relevance of this question --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: -- to this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will, and the reason is, it is not -- I think for this purpose the time is not critical. What I'm trying to have this witness assist you with is the attitudes or views of many of the Bosnian Croats - certainly not all - but toward people like Dario Kordic, and then a follow-up question concerning the man Tuta. And I think it is -- I think it is something the Chamber should know in terms of the way things were down there during this time, and perhaps still are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, if you're eventually going to lead us to the accused of this case, we'll allow you to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour, and I believe, I mean if I can predict -- I can't obviously completely predict how the witness will answer, but I believe I have four questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, we believe that it is highly improper to talk about what some people in Bosnia-Herzegovina felt three, four years, three years, two years after the facts which we've been hearing about since September 10th of last year in this Trial Chamber. It's unbelievable, and we object strongly to being able to allow this type of evidence so far after the scope of this indictment. We -- clear -- it's been pointed out that not only after the indictment, the war had been over with, peace had settled in, it was peacetime. It -- where does this end if we start this? I object strongly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, the statement about Mr. Kordic, that would be one of my next questions, was allowed in the Kordic case. I realise that's not governing on this Chamber. I fully appreciate that, but I simply point that out to Chamber. It was relevant to who the man Kordic was, and I -- all I suppose I can do is make an offer of proof that -- of what the evidence would be, and if you think it's relevant or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, you have to explain to us how relevant it is for that case with this very case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. Your Honour, this -- I believe that if -- I would put it -- I would make the offer of proof this way: That if allowed, I believe, from prior statements of this witness, the witness would indicate that this HVO senior official said to Mr. Garrod, he said, "You must remember -- you must remember that Kordic was our Churchill. He was a war hero to these people." And then I was going to ask Sir Martin if he had any similar information about how Tuta was regarded in the Mostar region, and I submit the witness, I expect, would say that he was regarded by a large number of the Bosnian Croats as a war hero. And I think the Chamber should know that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But why don't you ask a direct question concerning the accused rather than refer to another case?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, because I thought that it was appropriate because we've asked questions before about the HVO leadership and that this was not -- a position not unique to Mr. Naletilic but this was the attitude that many of these leaders were held in. I thought it was quite relevant. Of course, I wasn't allowed to ask the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, for your indulgence, but I want to object briefly but strongly, in the strongest possible terms. I cannot allow it, and I really strongly protest against introducing by the back door into the courtroom certain things which are happening outside the time frame. The war ended with the Washington Accords, which is in 1994, and then peace set in, and thank God it is still there. And there is the Federation which is still such as it is. This Court is not competent to try anything that happened during the time of peace. Our indictment ends with February, and what is more important with regard to this witness, and we've read his previous statement, all his knowledge about the events date from the -- from 1994, that is, following April 18th, that is, after the peace was established. And then in 1995, 1996, and so forth, when this witness, of course, was there and he was principally concerned to establish a united government in Mostar. Of course he heard a lot of hearsay. Of course there was a lot of grapevine; of course there were a lot of things, but that, Your Honours, has nothing to do with the indictment. What he heard in 1995, 1996, 1997 about the political interests, about the political struggles among political parties, that has nothing to do. What the witness knows about 1993, he has already told us. Thank you very much, Your Honours, but once again I protest in the strongest possible terms and I hope you will not allow it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may ask a question about how the accused in this case was regarded in 1993 and 1994 but not mention the other case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir Martin, if you recall, based on your experience and involvement in Herzegovina and the Mostar region in 1993 and certainly at least the first part of 1994, can you tell the Chamber your understanding and assessment of how many of the Bosnian Croat people regarded Mr. Naletilic?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say to about 50 per cent of the Croats that Mladen Naletilic was a mythical -- well, not mythical but a hero of the war, and they regarded him with respect and awe. I can give an example of that but the example is a little bit outside the time scale.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In light of the limitations, Sir Martin, I won't ask you about that. Sir Martin, I thank you very much for your testimony. No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any cross-examination? Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: My name is Chris Meek, and I am one of the Defence counsel for the accused Mladen Naletilic.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: The first question I have is how would you like me to address you?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't worry me at all. Anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir Martin, did you take a survey in 1995? You've just testified that 50 per cent of the Croats believed that my client was some hero of the war. Did you take a survey?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: How many people did you even talk to?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I talked to, over the years, to a lot of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You also indicated that out of these number of people that many of the people felt that he was a mythical person. Didn't you say that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think I took the word "mythical" back. I think they held him in "awe" is the word.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Would it surprise you, Sir Martin, if we've had one other witness in this case who has described Mr. Naletilic as a myth?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a myth. Well, to my mind, a myth is something which does not exist, whereas I think Mr. Naletilic does exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: While a person might be actually existing, his actions or his position could be mythical, couldn't they?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Certainly actions and -- ascribed to him could be --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- could be mythical, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you're aware, are you not, that Mr. Naletilic was involved in the war alongside his Muslim brothers against the Serb aggressors?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And isn't it a fair statement, Sir Martin, that these people who you have claimed believed him to be some sort of a mythical hero could very well have been describing their feelings toward this gentleman from the war against the Serb aggressors?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, indeed. And that applied to a number of other leaders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. If you'd like to look at the document, Sir Martin, you certainly can. It's 642, P642. It's a daily summary from 13 -- excuse me. Yeah, 13 of October, 1993. I don't think you really need to but -- you indicated in that report that there were two Muslim villages that were somehow being taken care or protected by my client Tuta, and you also indicated that you were very pleased to see or hear that; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. One was always delighted to hear of people of the opposite divide taking care of the minorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And do you have any knowledge of how many other villages in the area that my client may have had some protection or have taken care of other than these two?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You do not rule out that possibility, though, do you, Sir Martin?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You indicated in your direct examination, Sir Martin, that your goals with the ECMM were three, and I believe you even put them in the proper order -- correct me if I'm wrong -- political first, military -- military second, and third humanitarian.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Reporting on those three issues, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: If I'm pausing, Sir Martin, I'm trying to look at the transcript to make sure we don't overlap since we both speak the same language.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So -- do you mean by that statement that you were primarily interested in political matters in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were attempting to get -- I'm sorry. I must be a bit slower. Yes. We were attempting to gain for our masters, our political masters in the capitals, as an accurate picture as we possibly could of the political strands running throughout the whole of the country, because as you will be aware, at this time the Vance-Owen Plan was collapsing, but then we were moving on into other discussions, the Invincible plan, the EU action, and so on. So it was essential that all the political masters in our countries had as accurate information as possible on the political situation and, of course, the military situation which was so closely linked in with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So the lowest priority on your list was humanitarian aid, is that correct, or helping humanitarian convoys?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was third in the priorities but I would not say it was of a low priority, certainly not. It was of great importance to us, and we spent a great deal -- a great deal of our time on humanitarian matters. But as I said, it was the political and military reporting which were the first two priorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And when you indicated earlier that you were gaining this information on political matters and military matters for your masters, are you indicating the British government?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not indicating the British government. I'm indicating the -- well, for me, initially, the regional centre, then the headquarters of the ECMM, and from there to the EU Presidency and the capitals of the 12 countries and five OSCE countries that formed the EC monitor mission. I was not -- I must stress I was not reporting to the British government at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And, Sir Martin, tell me if you can, at that time in 1993, did Britain have any interests in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think we all -- I think Britain certainly, along with other countries, had a great deal of interest in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: What kind of interest would that have been, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Concern after the war in Slovenia and then the war in Croatia and to see a third war erupting in Bosnia. In other words, great concern and a determination to try and resolve the whole problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'll be quite honest with you, Sir Martin. Since you started your testimony on Monday afternoon, you've spoken about so many things and so many topics and so many areas that I really didn't even know where to start this cross-examination. So bear with me, please.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: If you know, can you tell us, me and the Trial Chamber, why it took so long for the western world to step into the situation in the Balkans back then, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I wonder how relevant that is, Your Honour. Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Meek, we don't believe this question is relevant. You must skip this question. It's too political.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Pardon me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It's too political oriented.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: The reason I asked it, Your Honour, Sir Martin has testified that his primary goal was political in his ECMM mission. I understand it's a political question, but he did testify to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you know, this is a Tribunal. We are just addressing the individual responsibilities rather than to solve any political issues, and this witness is certainly not a politician. He may be an expert in military matters, but certainly he's not a politician. So you must skip this question. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will skip this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir Martin, as the President, Judge Liu, just mentioned, you may be an expert in military matters, and my question to you is: Did you come to this Tribunal, in your own mind, to testify as a military expert?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout my whole time in Bosnia, I was not in a military role. First of all, with the EC monitor mission, we were civilians, and then for the rest of my time in Bosnia I was there in a civilian capacity, albeit having had a military background.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And a fairly lengthy and extensive military background at that, I take it. Thirty-seven years, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Are you then familiar with any rules concerning warfare or armed aggression between countries?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not be able to read off the various conventions, but I am -- I am aware, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'd like to pose a question then to you. If, for example, two countries are side by side, like Sweden and Norway, and Sweden acts as an aggressor and attacks Norway, are you aware of any rules, military rules of conduct which would allow Norway to move into the actual -- inside the borders of Sweden, the aggressors, in order to protect their country and neutralise the aggressors?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact rules, but I would have thought that if one is being attacked from another country, then you are entitled to take retaliatory action, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And in fact specifically, if you know, is it allowed to go into that other country, the aggressive country, in order to neutralise and take your troops into that country to neutralise, and in defence, the aggressor?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the rules say, but common sense says yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir Martin, I want to clarify the fact that your first posting in Bosnia was in Mostar on 1st of July, 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And it's my understanding that you arrived in Siroki Brijeg first.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were based -- CC headquarters was based in a little house in Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: It took -- was it two weeks before you finally got into Mostar or --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: -- four weeks?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it must have been the best part of six weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Six weeks?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hmm. I was trying every single day to get in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: During this six-week period, you came to know the chief of police of Siroki Brijeg, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I didn't come to know him. I think I had one meeting with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: The mayor of Siroki Brijeg, did you meet him?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: How many other approximate persons in government in Siroki Brijeg, in the municipal -- city level, did you meet?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very few, because I hardly spent any time in Siroki Brijeg. I did not realise at that time how many interesting people were living in Siroki Brijeg, otherwise I would have spent more time in Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Once you finally did arrive in Mostar and set up your headquarters, which under your testimony would be approximately six weeks; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We got into Mostar, but we didn't move the base from Siroki Brijeg because at that stage -- sorry. I'm just looking at the -- at that stage, it wasn't possible to find any accommodation for the headquarters in Mostar. So we were still based in Siroki Brijeg, travelling daily to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: After you were -- after you did get some headquarters in Mostar, you remained in Siroki Brijeg, though? You slept every night in Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: We left in Siroki Brijeg, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: During the whole 91 days that you were there, or 90 some-odd days that you were there; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Apart from my visits to Zenica, Zagreb, or wherever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: After the first ordeal that you've described, the difficulties of getting into Mostar proper, how many days on the average per week would you go into Mostar personally, Sir Martin?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is quite difficult to remember, but I would say two or three times a week into West Mostar and two or three times a week into East Mostar. That was the focus of our interest. Of course, I did have other responsibilities, but Mostar was the focus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir Martin, I notice you looking at the screen and the transcription has stopped, but I'm listening to the French translation. So that's why I'm waiting longer to ask my next question.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am -- that's all right. I'm trying to notice whether there are any --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you're trying to notice if there's any --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. No, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I forgot to mention this earlier so I'll ask it now before I forget. Which one of the three primary responsibilities of your ECMM mission, political, military, and humanitarian, which one of those fell into being a front man for BBC to get into East Mostar to make a documentary?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't suppose that they were really concerned -- you mean from my point of view?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of those. It didn't fall into any particular category. It was just a request that we had from the BBC to help them to get into Mostar, and we tried to assist international organisations, where we could, as we knew the ground and we had the contacts. So this was purely a response to a request.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: But not -- you'll agree with me that request came not from an international organisation or humanitarian organisation, though, did it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But we did -- we used to have many requests from many different people. Some we accepted; some we didn't. But this seemed to us to be a perfectly reasonable request, so we said we would do what we could to help them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Did you spend more time, in your opinion, in East Mostar or did you spend more time in West Mostar during that period of time that you would go two to three times a week?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say roughly 50/50.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber, please, what personal knowledge you have, not what someone told you or you read in any report, but what personal knowledge you have of the presence of HV troops in Mostar during your three months there?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I relied on reports of my teams who I had utmost faith in, but the only HV that I have told you that I actually saw were on the mountain road between Tomislavgrad and Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: For the benefit of the Trial Chamber, that's approximately how many hours away by car from Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you Tomislavgrad is about two hours, two hours by road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And Tomislavgrad is very close to the border of Croatia and Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's -- it's heading down towards Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: How far from the border between Croatia and Bosnia is Tomislavgrad located, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think driving time from the border to Tomislavgrad probably would have about three-quarters of an hour to an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I believe most all of the attorneys in this courtroom, including you, Sir Martin, have been to this area. The Trial Chamber has not. So when you describe a 30 or 45-minute drive, these are on small, windy roads and not super highways or autobahns; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's a reasonable tarmac road up from Split to Tomislavgrad but then from Tomislavgrad to Prozor, it was a totally -- a mountain track.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see you've already pulled out the map. I'm simply going to suggest that it might assist the witness and the Chamber to have one of the maps, in particular I've pulled out P3, but I think it makes it much clearer than just talking about it abstractly, I submit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I would like to thank my learned colleague for that suggestion, and if I could borrow the map P --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sure. You can use me or the Registry's. It doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: -- P3 for the ELMO, please. For the record, we have a map previously identified and admitted as P3 in front of Sir Martin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: If you'd like to, Sir Martin, certainly feel free to take the map in your hand and look at it first, if you'd like to.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And once you have found the location of Tomislavgrad, you might circle that.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's marked -- it's marked on the map as Duvno.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. While you still have the map, Sir Martin, could you do me another favour? Does that map reflect the boundary of the country of Croatia on Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Can you take that red pen that you have in your hand and draw the line where the border is, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We have no objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Scott, please. Mr. Scott, your microphone. You could not be interpreted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks] Sorry. Can I just mark on one more thing? [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Sir Martin. You have a pointer there --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: -- somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: The usher will have a --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wait a minute. There is Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tomislavgrad, marked "Duvno" on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the mountain road was between Tomislavgrad and Prozor, up through the mountains here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this, I think you might just be able to see it, I have marked it --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I see it very clearly. Thank you, Sir Martin. So that would be, as the crow flies, from Tomislavgrad to the border of Croatia, can you roughly give us an estimate of the kilometres since you spent so much time there?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used to think in terms of time, not distance, because distance didn't make -- wasn't relevant. It was time. I would say about three-quarters of an hour. I'd say about --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: As the crow --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- 45 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: As the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Something like that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. I don't need the ELMO any longer.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe a little bit more. Maybe a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir Martin, you were -- you didn't discuss this in your direct testimony, but most of the ECMM personnel and other monitors who have testified in this Trial Chamber have described being briefed before they went to the area on their mission. Were you also briefed?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had a briefing in London because I was recruited by our foreign office initially and then flew out to Zagreb, where we were given briefings on the whole of the former Yugoslavia at the headquarters of the ECMM, because at that stage we did not know where we were going to go. We were asked where we wanted to go. I said Bosnia, and I fortunately got it, so then went to Zenica where I had further briefings. But I did not know for -- I was a week in Zenica, at the regional centre, and then I was told that the head wanted me to go down to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Would it be a fair statement, Sir Martin, that when you were briefed in London, in Zagreb, in Zenica, that you were briefed on all of the political climate as you might find it in this area around Mostar? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically around Mostar. London was a very broad briefing on the whole of the Yugoslavia. In Zagreb, the ECMM operations areas were described, but again covering it in big detail but not focusing -- Mostar was not -- I suppose it must have been discussed, but it wasn't in detail. And it wasn't until I got to Zenica that we started talking about specific areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. I presume that would be the way it would work. So in Zenica is when you learned and were briefed the clearest and in the most detail about what to expect militarily, politically, and otherwise on the ground in Mostar and in that south-west Herzegovina area; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And in those briefings, you were told, were you not, the political figures and the military figures of the ABiH army and their -- and the HVO; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose I was, but I can't really remember what those briefings consisted of, because what really matters is not what you're told but when you get on the ground and see what the situation is yourself. So I have Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to say that a lot of those briefings I had in London, Zagreb, even in Zenica, may have faded away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So even in Zenica when you had a week long -- you were there for one week approximately in your briefing before going to Mostar, you don't have an independent recollection of asking questions of, "Which individuals should I speak with in the HVO," or "Which individuals should I speak with in the ABiH army"?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You don't remember it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember it. What really mattered was when I got on the ground talking to my predecessor, talking to him directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And your predecessor was?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Claus Nissen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So that Claus gave you the best briefing once you reached the ground in Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the most immediate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just noticed that it is break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, will you please show the witness out of the room first. We will resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir Martin, a quick question about your predecessor there in Siroki Brijeg or Mostar, Claus. How long had he been there before you relieved him?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, that I couldn't answer accurately. I think about three or four months.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: In the broad -- in the broad briefing you received in London you've just described earlier this afternoon, you learned, did you not, that the country of Croatia was attacked by the aggressors, the JNA, the Serbian army, in 1991 and 1992 through the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina into southern Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware that there was a war going on indeed in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you were aware indeed that it was the Serbian aggressors coming through Bosnia-Herzegovina to attack Croatia in the southern part?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the precise routes they used to get to Vukovar, but I wasn't aware that that -- it could have been through Bosnia, but I wasn't aware of the precise routes, but Vukovar, of course, is adjoining Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you mean Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think at this -- if these questions and answers are to have any meaning or relevance at all, we need to have both time and location as to particular events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Meek, what is your follow-up questions? Are you going to lead us to the international armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may continue, but bear in mind the objections from the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir Martin, are you aware of the agreement called the Split agreement which was reached, I think, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of it but I can't remember precisely what that agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. You indicated in your direct testimony, Sir Martin, that you, during your time in Bosnia and in the Mostar area, that you did not visit the Heliodrom; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I visited it but wasn't able to get inside it. I tried to but did not succeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Were you aware or are you aware that one of your -- one of your people from M2 actually visited the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he did, I can't remember when.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You've indicated in your direct testimony, Sir Martin, that you used different sources, correct, for your information?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Can you give me some examples of these sources, please?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Talking to Croats, talking to Bosniaks, talking to Serbs, and of course talking to members of the international organisations and NGOs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Were there any specific sources that you used on a regular basis that -- that you can tell us about?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My main sources, my main sources were direct information from Croat political and military leaders and Bosniak political and military leaders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Did you have personally an interpreter while you were in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And can you tell me the nationality or ethnicity of that interpreter?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: We used Croat interpreters in West Mostar, but when we went over to East Mostar, we would use a Bosniak interpreter because the -- otherwise, the interpreters would not be acceptable if they were the wrong side of the River Neretva.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Did you use -- excuse me. Did you use your interpreters as sources?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not really, because apart from factual information of localities and how to contact individuals and so on, we did not draw them into any form of political discussions. It would have been unfair on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Did you just say that it would be unfair to use your interpreters as sources?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me the approximate number of meetings you had with Croats versus the number of meetings you had with Muslims during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that three months?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably had more meetings with Croats because we were living on the Croat side, as I say, in Siroki Brijeg. All our early dealings were with Croat leaders, trying to get into Mostar, which didn't leave all that much time by the time we got into East Mostar for the Bosniaks. So it would have been inevitably more meetings with the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: In regards to this BBC documentary which you helped to organise, can you tell me whether or not there was any filming done on the west side of Mostar or was it solely on the east side?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I correct you? I did not help to organise it. All I did was discuss it with Praljak and then I personally led them over into East Mostar and left them there. But what they were going to do, that was their business.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Would "facilitate" have been a better word, Sir Martin?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Facilitate, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. To your knowledge, did Jeremy Bowen pass through the west side of Mostar to reach the east side to film this documentary?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He would have to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. And again, if you know, and if you don't please tell me, do you know if Jeremy Bowen and his crew did any filming on the west side of Mostar while they were there?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge. Certainly the focus of the film is the situation in East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yesterday, in your direct testimony, or perhaps the day before, you had indicated that there were many Croats in Herzegovina who called Tudjman as their president; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Did this confirm to you in any fashion that the Croats living in Herzegovina did not accept - excuse me - Mr. Izetbegovic as their lawful president?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is certainly the impression that I gained. As far as they were concerned, their president was Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And do you know of any specific reasons why they felt that way?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was a very close link between the Croats of Bosnia and Croatia. As I've said, there were a number of members of Tudjman's government who came from Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you know, Sir Martin, how many Croatian citizens were born in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: How many Croatia citizens, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Were born in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: If I told you 400.000 approximately, would that ring any bells?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wouldn't ring a bell, but it wouldn't surprise me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And the total population of Croatia, to your knowledge, is approximately 4 million; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir Martin, if you can tell me, and you may not be able to, do you know how many citizens -- excuse me, how many Muslims have citizenship in the country of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir Martin, are you aware that all Croatians who live anywhere in the world, such as the United States where I come from, such as Great Britain where you come from, can hold a dual citizenship?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would not surprise me, no. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And with this dual citizenship, under the parliamentary law of Croatia and the constitution of Croatia, these citizens are allowed to vote in Croatian elections through the Croatian embassies. Are you aware of that, Sir Martin?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the assumption, presumably, that they were Croatian, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You are aware of that then?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, dual citizenship Croatia and the United States, dual passport, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes. And it's not -- nothing uncommon about having a dual citizenship, is it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I was referring to Croats from Bosnia having Croatian passports and voting in the Croatian elections. Not Croatian, Croats from Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Were you aware that a Croatian who has a dual citizenship can even run for an elected office even though they're not physically living in the country of Croatia at the time they're running for election?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That wouldn't surprise me, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You spoke yesterday and the day before about certain meetings that were had where you describe Croatian politicians being present at those meetings, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And Sir Martin, were you somewhat surprised because of this?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't surprised, because we realised the very strong effects that Croatia had on the Croats of Bosnia, and indeed we used to consult with the Croatian government, Tudjman, Granic, and so on, to assist us in our task in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Which leads me and probably answers my next question, and that is: Is it your understanding and is it not true that during this period of time the European Community was requesting the help of certain Croatian politicians in helping to solve this conflict, this civil war?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: We in Mostar certainly consulted Tudjman, Granic, and others to assist us in our task, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Meek, you have to slow down a little bit. The French interpretation is far behind you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I apologise to Judge Diarra. I'm sorry. The only way I can tell if the French is finished... [French interpretation on the English Channel]

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir Martin, you had spoke -- excuse me, you testified yesterday or the day before about a meeting held in Medjugorje where President Tudjman was present. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't -- I don't know. I don't recall that one, but certainly it wouldn't surprise me. But I don't recall that specific meeting, unless it's in this folder.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Perhaps it was the Grude meeting that you were attending.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Grude meeting, certainly Tudjman was not present in Grude. That was Mate Granic, the Foreign Minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yesterday or the day before, Sir Martin, you testified about the presence of Mujahedin, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Can you tell me and tell this Trial Chamber, please, what countries these Mujahedin were coming from?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: From a whole variety of Islamic countries. I personally thought it was a great mistake that they were ever allowed into the country, and I think others did too. I used to raise this subject on many occasions with the Bosniak Generals in Central Bosnia, most of whom did not want the Mujahedin either, and -- but they assured me that they had them under control, but I was not all that convinced.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Such as yesterday or the day before, you testified that the HVO was giving you what you've called excuses of certain factions that were out of control and that you believe that it was a weak or lame excuse. Wasn't that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I did say that all sides occasionally claimed they had out of control elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And, Sir Martin, would this be one example of an ABiH general perhaps or some military person telling you that the Mujahedin are out of control and it's their fault?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall any specific instant, although of course the hijacking of our team up near Jablanica by the Mujahedin, I don't think that was ordered by the ABiH generals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So it would be a fair statement, Sir Martin, that on both sides, the ABiH and the HVO, had at times factions that they couldn't control?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true, but I never accepted it as an excuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, these same variety of mid-east countries that were sending Mujahedin into Bosnia to fight were also sending weapons into Bosnia, isn't that a fact? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no doubt, because, of course, there was the arms embargo on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir Martin, these same countries that were sending Mujahedin and sending weapons to Bosnia were also sending financial aid to the ABiH, were they not?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no proof of that, but I think it's very possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Can you give me and this Trial Chamber your opinion of what these people, these Mujahedin fighters, what were they fighting for?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: With hindsight, some sort of Islamic cause, but I never established while I was there precisely what they were there for. Maybe just to help their Muslim brothers. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you believe they were there to fight for a multi-ethnic Bosnia, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that they were probably there to come and support the Muslim cause in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You haven't testified specifically to your military experience other than it was 37 years, but you have been in other theatres of combat in that 37 years. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And would you agree that in Bosnia in 1993 when you were there, and in -- as in previous countries where there were war conflicts where you were present, that rumours and stories travel fast?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And in particular, the comparison I make -- I used to make was between Mostar and Belfast.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that during this time in Bosnia and the civil war that these stories would often, as is human nature, become distorted and become more grandiose in the telling of the same?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And of course there was a considerable amount of media disinformation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Sir Martin, with all that in mind, is it so far out of your realm of possibility to believe that the story of the kidnapping of the ECMM people, the armed robbery of their Mercedes at gunpoint by these Mujahedin, might very well in the telling of this story become something to the effect that the Mujahedin were killing children and raping women throughout Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I haven't quite got your point there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I think we've agreed on several things. One is that stories and rumours tend to fly in war and that's what happened in Bosnia; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, rumours did proliferate. That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: The second is it is a fact that the ECMM team, I think it was M1, was or were the victims of kidnapping, armed robbery at gunpoint; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Isn't it reasonable, Sir Martin, that a story, a factual story such as that, including Mujahedin, could in the telling evolve itself into a story that the Mujahedin were raping women and killing children?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't quite see how that -- that case could have happened, because the report was to us, and this was an internal matter, not to the Croats. I don't think the Croats were even aware that this had happened. I don't think they were aware. It is a matter of considerable embarrassment to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Of course. But the fact is, and you'll have to agree, I think, that that story could have got out in many ways?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have got out, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have an estimate, Sir Martin, of the number of Mujahedin fighters in Bosnia, Central Bosnia you talked about yesterday and south-west Bosnia-Herzegovina, during that time period?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but my estimate -- I guessed it was in the region of hundreds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you will agree with me, Sir Martin, that it takes far less than a hundred fundamentalist Islamic radicals to cause a lot of damage, as we saw on September 11th in New York?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, certainly. I agree. That's why I said I think it was a terrible mistake to ever have allowed them in in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So my question -- are we going too fast?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are we now in the field covered by the indictment, Mr. Meek, or are we now trying to have a historical background about how Muslims show solidarity vis-a-vis their Muslim brothers throughout the world?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I couldn't hear the translation. I had to read it. Your Honour, we are in the area covered by the direct examination yesterday and the day before by the Prosecutor's Office where the Mujahedin was brought up, number one. Number two, we're into the area of dealing with the direct examination and documents that were put to this witness about exaggerated concerns by the Croats of Mujahedin warriors in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we have spent a lot of time on the Mujahedin issues, but we still don't know where you are leading us to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And more than anything else, I don't believe that it is relevant to speak about 11th of September and what happened in the US. This only happened very recently and is of no relevance to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. Thank you, Your Honours. The relevance of this question I want to ask Sir Martin --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: In some of the reports we have seen in this binder, there is talk about the fact that the Croats in Herzegovina were constantly talking about their fear of the Mujahedin and that the belief by the ECMM was that these beliefs were unfounded. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear many concerns expressed about the Mujahedin as such. It was more, many times more, the prospect of an Islamic fundamentalist state.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir Martin, in this Trial Chamber since this trial started, we have had some testimony from another witness concerning a location called Bocina. Have you heard of Bocina?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name rings a bell, but I'm afraid I can't picture it on the map or what happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, it was a training camp for Mujahedin in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Does that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that does now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Were you ever made aware that President Izetbegovic was in that camp giving these Mujahedin support and even he got some honours from them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I've been quiet over here, but I think this has now gone on for some time. What is the relevance of this? If they can connect this to a defence, to a defence to the charges in the indictment, perhaps it should go on, but it is not clear to me it has any relevance at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We quite agree with you, Mr. Scott. I don't think this issue has some relevance to the -- to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: May I, if Your Honour permits me, I believe the relevance is simply that this witness has testified from his knowledge of being on his mission in Bosnia that the Croats did not accept President Izetbegovic as being the legal president of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I'm trying to get at and question this witness as to the reasons why the Croats may not have accepted Izetbegovic as the lawful president.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, counsel. Assuming for the moment that that's true, assuming there were Croats in Herzegovina who did not accept President Izetbegovic as their legitimate leader, I would ask the Chamber to ask the Defence, how is that a defence to the charges in that case? Does that allow prisoners to be used as human shields? Does that allow mosques to be destroyed? How is it relevant to a defence to the charges in the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have heard my learned colleague from the other side just now indicate to Your Honours that, to make it short, I think, to cut to the chase, that every question in cross-examination has to be related to the defence, and I don't believe that's correct. I believe that in cross-examination I'm allowed to ask anything that was dealt with in direct examination. And they dealt with this in direct examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But the baseline is the relevance to this very case. We have spent a lot of time on the Mujahedin issues, and we have been sitting here for more than four months. We believe that that issue, the Mujahedin issue, is only a very small portion in this case. You must skip these questions and continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir Martin --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Meek -- sorry -- there is no dispute on this issue. I think everybody in the Court accepts that there were Mujahedin in the area of conflict in Bosnia and that obviously their presence fuelled flames, but that's not in dispute. There's no point cross-examining on something that we all agree with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm glad that we all agree on that now. I'm off that subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir Martin, during your direct testimony, you spent some time testifying about your knowledge, albeit secondhand or thirdhand, of expulsions of Muslims from the west bank of Mostar to the east bank. Do you recall that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Can you give us an estimate of the -- or give us an estimate or any information on the number of Croats who were expelled to the east bank from the west bank?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a very interesting matter. There were very, very few Croats in east Mostar. I never established precisely when they moved across, but it is possible. One of the theories I always had was perhaps they were directed by the HVO to move across before the shelling of East Mostar started. I never had any evidence given to me about Croats being expelled from East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So then would it be a fair statement that you were not aware of the fact that there were only 12 Croats who stayed in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have put it more like 50, because there was still a number of mixed marriages, but the numbers were certainly very small.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And would you agree with me that there were approximately 9.000 Muslims living on the west bank of Mostar during this time period?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that again is an interesting figure. You see, the Croats used to say there were 9.000. The Bosniaks used to say there were 3.000. I used to split the difference in all the briefings I gave and talked about some 6.000. But there were a substantial number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And -- and if you know, Sir Martin, prior to 9 May of 1993, who was taking care of these refugees and displaced persons in West Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was still -- the Croats were inevitably the largest percentage in West Mostar, but the Croats were certainly dealing with a lot of refugees and DPs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you, Sir Martin, know anything at all about the ownership of apartments in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a lot of dealings with this because of the expellings which continued until 1996 and of which Vinko Martinovic, in my view, was largely responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you for that non-responsive answer. The question I'll ask you again, Sir Martin, do you have any knowledge of the ownership of the apartments in Mostar during your time there in the three months you spent in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what you mean by "ownership."

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
