utterances.text: Common term of ownership. Do you know who owned the apartments? Were people just taking apartments? Were --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Well, there had, up until the war, been clear tenancy agreements run by the municipal council, and of course there were some private houses. But after the war and during the war, that all broke down and it became completely bedlam.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I want to ask you a question about the Heliodrom. Can you please tell us, if you can, the percentage of detainees in the Heliodrom that were actually from Mostar as opposed to the detainees from other locations?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm very sorry. I was just checking that. I wonder if you -- could you possibly repeat that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: The question was, Sir Martin, if you can tell us, do you know the percentage of detainees in the Heliodrom, during your term there, that were actually from Mostar as opposed to detainees from other locations?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I do not have a breakdown, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I believe that it's in one of your reports -- it's a fair statement, isn't it, Sir Martin, that there were approximately 200.000 displaced Muslim refugees living in Croatia during 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were living in Croatia. There were certainly some 200.000 displaced Muslim refugees, some of them down in the south. Yes, I don't know exactly how many in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You mentioned that, in your opinion, that this predicament or conflict or civil war which you found yourself as a monitor in in 1993 all revolved around territory. Was that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my belief. Territory and population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And would you agree with me, Sir Martin, that there were large amounts of displaced persons coming into the Mostar area in the south-west Herzegovina area during this period of time and prior to your coming?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, particularly from Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And I believe -- and I believe that you -- in one of your reports, you've indicated that there may have been 20.000 to 30.000 Bosnian Croats who were displaced from Central Bosnia that had moved down to this area.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Further, that the Muslim refugees who were displaced because of the Serb aggression could have amounted to 10.000 to 20.000 also?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't have the precise figures, but that sounds about right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That in and of itself created most, if not all, of the problems Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that you experienced or you saw while you were in Bosnia; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The problem of DPs was one of our biggest problems of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You mentioned yesterday some names of some HVO military figures who you called hard-liners. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I don't believe you mentioned in your testimony about any hard-line ABiH military personnel, but there were some, were there not?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but they were more up in Sarajevo, not quite so much in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: What about Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zenica, the generals I had dealings with up there were mainly concerned with fighting the war, and we used to discuss endlessly their war aims, but they insisted that they were fighting for a unified Bosnia. But many -- I can go on if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'm just waiting, Sir Martin, for the transcript to catch up with us.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Please go ahead. I would like to hear your response.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the -- the Bosniak generals were very determined, during the time I was there, to regain the territory that they'd lost, in particular, to the Serbs. I'm talking about Zvornik, the upper reaches of the River Drina, Sanski Most, Prijedor, access to the Sava in the north, access to the Adriatic via Neum in the south, and indeed all those areas which before the fighting they had held the majority. So the Bosniak generals were extremely determined.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Would you agree, Sir Martin, that if the ABiH wanted to reach the Adriatic Sea, they would have to have taken Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, they would have to have taken Gornji Vakuf and then Prozor. That is why I mentioned, I think this morning, Prozor was just a key town for the Croats. They would have to have taken Gornji Vakuf, which was divided between the Bosniaks and the Croats -- I'm sorry, I'm going too fast -- then Prozor, then down to Mostar, and from Mostar south to the sea.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So the -- the precise answer to that last question was yes, they would have had to have taken Mostar, in addition to these other two locations that you've mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Although the main road, the main road coming down, the M17 road, actually just continues down the east side of the Neretva and so in fact passes through the Bosniak side of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You mentioned this -- you mentioned General Arif Pasalic, I think yesterday and the day before.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You indicated, I believe, that you believed him to be an honourable man.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never had any reason to doubt it. He was concerned with fighting the war, and I didn't hear him say any -- make any remarks which I considered not acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Wasn't he one of the generals that you had indicated said that he would fight to the end, if need be?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Was he not one of the generals who would be a hard-liner?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I draw a distinction between military people who say they're going to fight and fight and fight until they achieve their objectives. When I say hard-liners, I'm more talking about the political side, the political side, political aims, bearing in mind, as I said, that the political side and the military side frequently overlapped.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And that overlapping that you've spoken about and testified to occurred in both armies, the HVO and the ABiH; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I would talk to politicians and we would discuss military matters and vice versa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: When did you first meet Arif, General Pasalic?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met him, I suppose, on the first day when I got across into East Mostar, which must have been the latter part of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And was he one of the first ABiH generals that you met and spoke with?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was the only one in the south. That was the four corps area. So he was the only one I could meet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until I went up to Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Right. So prior to your -- I'll start this question this way: You were in Zagreb, then in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Or Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Prior to your reaching Siroki Brijeg, you had not spoken with any ABiH generals; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you didn't speak with any ABiH generals until you met Pasalic in East Mostar sometime in August 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Sir Martin, yesterday you indicated that you first met my client, Tuta, on August 15th of 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you believed him to be upset because you had to ask him his name twice and it meant nothing to you; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you indicated in your testimony that when he expressed his views on the state of affairs as concerned Muslims in that region, that you tried to tell him the generals that you had drank brandy with scoffed at that idea of a fundamental Islamic state, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say you're absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: But can I just say one thing?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Sir Martin.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I just add one thing? I think, if you look at my actual report, you will see I use the word "Muslims" and not "generals." And I certainly had spoken to Muslims in Zenica, but I hadn't met any generals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Sir Martin. I believe the record and transcript from yesterday's testimony will speak for itself. You talked about in your direct testimony ethnic cleansing, this word "ethnic cleansing"; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of any ethnic cleansing where Croats were cleansed?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Are they in any of the reports that you have been submitted and been reviewed in the last two or three days in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, because some of those -- some of the cases in Central Bosnia, in particular, took place before I arrived in Central Bosnia, towns like Bugojno, Fojnice and so on, Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: For the record, I believe line 17, Your Honours, on page 49, line 18 is missing, but I think the question was properly understood by the witness and it was: Do you have any knowledge of incidents where Muslims were ethnically cleansing Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you see that, Sir Martin?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Is that how you understood the question?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I said yes. Yes. Cleansing because some of those -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. We are going to look at a few documents, if you don't mind. Document 553.1.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: It's a daily summary from August 1, 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Under your signature; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And in that report under "Military activity," you speak about a meeting with Colonel Andabak, commander of the HVO special forces; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: This was --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Clearly a mis -- I got the terminology wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: The terminology wrong?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: His name is spelt incorrectly and his appointment incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Pardon me?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: And his appointment incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, it was to the best of your knowledge at the time on August 1st of 1993 that on Colonel Andabak was the commander of the HVO special forces, or you would not have put that in your report, would you?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I might have been advised incorrectly. I'd clearly been given the wrong information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Or you could have been given the correct information. Isn't that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible, but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you were given incorrect information, Sir Martin, how many times did that happen, that incorrect information was given to you and put in these reports and sent on up the chain?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Undoubtedly, it would have happened occasionally, but I hope very seldom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Hopefully not daily; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. I take it, Sir Martin, that during your time in Bosnia and specifically the three months you were there in Siroki Brijeg, in Mostar area, that you were trying to create an atmosphere of trust among all the parties so you could deal with them?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And in that attempt to create that trust, you tried to be as honest as you could with everybody, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: If you'll look at Exhibit P565.2 for a moment, Sir Martin?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And this again, this is the document that refers to your first meeting, first knowledge of my client, Tuta, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you indicate, did you not -- and I'll take you to the second page of that document -- you indicated that you didn't trust him, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And from reading your comment, it appeared that part of the reason that you didn't trust him or he was suspect was because he had a nickname. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a -- a jokey remark, but I tend to judge people on first meeting them. Sometimes I'm right, occasionally I'm wrong, but I like to think that usually my first impressions are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And that's just human nature, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: We all want to be right, don't we?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So we know now that in at least one of these documents you're now saying you had misinformation; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because in here I've called Mladen Naletilic commander of the HVO special forces. So there can't be two.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: So one of them is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And in another document you're putting jokes in it, is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure you will agree or you can see that that first sentence is meant to be, meant to be humorous. It may not have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Are you aware, Sir Martin, that there are many, many people in Bosnia-Herzegovina who have nicknames?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you tend to not trust these people because they have nicknames?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on who they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Going up a little -- a little down from there, you indicated that Tuta was definitely charismatic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You also indicated that further discussions with Tuta could prove interesting or indeed valuable; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You intended to use my client without letting him know that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends what you mean by "use." I was talking to anyone who could further our information and knowledge of the political, military, and other situation in Bosnia. I spent a great deal of my years in Bosnia talking to people whom I did not like, but that did not stop me talking to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You never spoke with Tuta after the 15th of August, 1993, did you?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We had a brief -- a brief -- we ran into each other briefly in the Hotel Ero when Tuta was having supper with someone else, but otherwise, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And that's in no report that you ever gave to the OTP, is it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: The fact that you ran into Tuta after the 15th of August, 1993, is not contained in any report that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor, is it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, none of these ECMM reports, no, because I'm talking about 1996, 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'm referring to the statements that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor, your formal statements. Do you recall, Sir Martin, that you first spoke with Mr. Carry Spork and Mr. Ramlal Goonewardene for three days in February 1998? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: The 17th, 18th, and the 19th, three days?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You reviewed this report, this official statement to the OTP, before you came to The Hague to testify, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: The first report is 16 pages long, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You didn't mention my client one time in 16 pages in three days of debriefing by the OTP, did you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, if there's going to be questioning about the document, I ask that it be put before the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I can do that but he said he reviewed the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Would you like to look through it again or do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he was mentioned in the document because this is a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. How many times did you meet with Slobodan Praljak, the chief general of the HVO or military?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was the only real proper meeting I had with him. As far as I can remember, he had only taken over his post not long before and then he was dismissed from his post a week after the destruction of the Stari Most, the old bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And wasn't it Mr. Roso who took his place after that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ante Roso, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Ante. Do you recall about what month that was?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he left his post?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can tell you exactly. The Stari Most was destroyed on the 9th of November, so a week later must make it about the 16th of November that he left that post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: At that time you were not posted in Mostar; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir Martin, in your direct testimony, you described in a little bit of detail about your conversation with my client, Tuta, on August 15th of 1993. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the views that he expressed to you concerning his fears of a fundamentalist Islamic state being created was -- was not -- wasn't something you'd never heard before?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, indeed, and of course I heard it from the Roman Catholic Church.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Exactly. It wasn't such an eccentric point of view, was it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, if we could look at document P359 for a moment. You found it, Sir Martin?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You found it quicker than I did. You mention in that report, bottom of page 1, last paragraph, about multiplication of Croatian flag raising in sensitive areas. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I could just point out that this is actually a report written by the head of the regional centre Zenica, Jean-Pierre Thebault, and it was the 1st of May, which is two months before I arrived in Bosnia. Now, yesterday I was testifying whether certain things in here still applied, and I said yes, but now you're looking at that particular paragraph, I don't know precisely the circumstances surrounding the flag raising in -- in Travnik, but I am aware that all people in Bosnia are very prone to raise their flags at every opportunity. So I don't know the significance of that, unless it had been put on a mosque, but it doesn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Right. And you'd agree with me that there's nothing inherently significant about flying a flag, is there?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes. We had awful problems over the years with flags.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: What about the -- let me ask this question --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: And in fact, we had to cancel the opening of two bridges built by the EU because we insisted no national flags.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: On either side, I presume?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: On either side. And because they were put up, no opening, cancelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: What year -- what year was that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're now talking about 1995, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you aware during your three months in Bosnia of any problems with the Croat flag flying?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I did say, we had an awful lot of problems with Croat flag flying, but you're saying when I was in Mostar at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, sir, Sir Martin.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course I was in -- no, I was not aware of any problems at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You mention in your direct testimony about school textbooks, I think. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that might have been a report by my predecessor, but I'm delighted to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Are you aware, Sir Martin, that before the war all textbooks came from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I was aware of that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Were you also aware that the Bosniak language was not established until 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Excuse me. 1998. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know there are people in this courtroom who will not agree with me, but as far as I'm concerned as an amateur linguist, they're all the same language.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Sir Martin. Let me ask you a quick question about the HVO and the ABiH armies in 1993. Did they have the same uniform, basically?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: They started off with the same uniform but then rapidly, I think it was sometime in 1993, they changed, and the HVO adopted the Croatian style army uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Was it after -- in 1993, after you had left Mostar for Zenica that this occurred?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be precise. I cannot be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: We've had some testimony from some other military figures in this courtroom, and I'm not sure if any of them have had as much military background as you have, but would you agree with me, Sir Martin, that in this crazy mixed-up civil war in Bosnia in 1993, that it was difficult to tell the three armies apart at times because of the uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to add that I don't consider it a civil war in Bosnia, but that's besides the point. No. At times, at times it was difficult to differentiate from a distance, but as soon as one got reasonably close, then it became apparent either through shoulder flashes or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I think, Mr. President, Your Honours, it's time for a break. I apologise for running us over a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Usher, would you show the witness out of the room, first. And in the meantime, may I ask Mr. Meek how long are you going to take after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've got a few more --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: It shouldn't take very long. It shouldn't take an hour -- microphone. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I don't want to tell the Trial Chamber something that I'm going to prove to be wrong, but I don't believe it will take me more than 20, 30 minutes at the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. You know, we have to make the logistic arrangements if we are not sitting tomorrow. If we have to sit, we have to inform the security, the Registry, to make the proper arrangements for tomorrow's sitting. So, Mr. Par, do you have any cross-examination and how long will it take?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the answer is yes, and it might take about one hour, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll resume at quarter to six.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir Martin, if we could look at Exhibit P559 for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That is a document dated 4 August 1993, a special report under the name of Jean Pierre Thebault; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Would you please look at page 2, paragraph 2 under subsection A/?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And just read the first sentence, if you would, please. Not out loud but look at it, please. Now, Sir Martin, that document indicates that at least on 4 August 1993, that the situation of about 30.000 to 40.000 civilians seized in Mostar since about three months (meaning far before any BiH army attacks anywhere). Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about from mid-May to mid-August. I can't recall, I'm afraid -- June, July -- May, June, July -- when the BiH military military offensive operations started.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Let me try to refresh your recollection, sir. Sir Martin, are you aware of the March 1993 BiH attack on Konjic?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. But you're aware of it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you aware, Sir Martin, of the April 1993 BiH attack on Trusina?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember where Trusina is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you aware of the, I believe March 1993, attack by the BH army on Orliste?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm afraid this is before my time. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Could it be possible that this is one of those instances where Jean-Pierre Thebault had been given bad information, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot really answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if you'll look at the same document, sir, on page 2 under subsection B.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: The second sentence talks about these operations followed -- have followed the mutiny of Muslim soldiers of the HVO and have given the opportunity to the BH army to create a horseback quarter between Jablanica and Mostar. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: My question, if you know, did the ABiH army have sleepers in the HVO, soldiers that were -- had alliances with the BH army but in fact turned their weapons on the HVO at an appropriate time, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course, until the fighting started, the Muslims were fully involved in the HVO, and of course they fought together in the HVO with the HVO against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And at some --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: And so there were Muslims in the HVO forces, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Can you confirm or do you have any knowledge that in fact some of these Muslim soldiers in the HVO were in fact sleepers, so to speak, who were just waiting for the appropriate time to mutiny?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't put it like that. I would say that when the fighting started, then they had -- they knew where their loyalties lay, and these were the -- these particular ones were the Muslims in the HVO, the barracks in East Mostar which then was taken over by the ABiH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, you spoke briefly about the bad conditions in East Mostar and lack of water and food; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Are you aware, Sir Martin, that during the time period of at least perhaps June of 1993 in West Mostar that the HVO was rationing water in West Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: They may have been rationing water, but at least they had water to ration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. And you indicated that you didn't really have a good answer or understanding as to why the HVO were taking detainees to the island; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Couldn't it very well have been and were you ever made aware of the possibility that there was a shortage of food because of this massive influx of displaced persons?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was certainly -- it was certainly part of the release procedure and certainly the ICRC noted that with the 500 gone out at Dretelj the conditions for the remainder were better.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Bear with me, Sir Martin, and we'll get finished pretty quickly, I think. Yesterday you spoke about the shelling of East Mostar when you were there. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You also testified that the Serbs were still shelling Mostar, the east side mainly, during this period.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You can't tell us today, can you, what mosques might have been destroyed by the Serb shelling as opposed to the HVO shelling, can you?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, indeed. And of course, the Serb shelling was not nearly so regular at this stage, but certainly all the bridges, all the bridges in Mostar had been destroyed during the fighting with the Serbs. That is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: What evidence do you have that the Serb shelling was not -- did not result in the destruction or damage to some or all mosques in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is conceivable that some of the Serb shelling may have damaged -- certainly damaged buildings and may have damaged mosques. That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much, sir. You mentioned yesterday in your testimony concerning the Vance-Owen Peace Plan that the Croatian or the Croats had a misunderstanding of this Vance-Owen Peace Plan?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my interpretation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You also testified that most all of -- or all the Croats you spoke to sang the same tune. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Will you agree with me that during your tenure in Bosnia that the many times you spoke with members of the BiH army, that they also sang the same tune, so to speak, that they were the victims, they were the poor victims?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: But, but I should add that they did consistently say they did want a unified Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Speaking of that, you've testified in this Tribunal before, at least one time; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Just once?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just once.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Have you been requested by the OTP to testify in any other cases besides this case?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I've got some indications that some lawyers want to speak to me about possible other cases. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: OTP lawyers?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: OTP. What does OTP --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. I think so, yes. But I have no idea what they wish to speak to me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yesterday, you were speaking about Dario Kordic and your regular dealings with Mr. Kordic and his views. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You testified that there was almost an identical or general theme. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you also testified that you believe that Dario Kordic had close links to Boban; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe he was related, but I may be wrong there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Correct. So you also testified that no doubt Kordic's views reflected Boban's views because they had close links. Wasn't that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Isn't that, in a fashion, guilt by association? Because someone has close links, they must have the same opinion?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I was aware that Boban was an extremely strong nationalist. He was the creator of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna and therefore it was only natural that the people he placed in positions of authority would reflect his views.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You testified yesterday that there was a joke while you were in Bosnia, and you said it in Croatian, but it meant "Thank you, Vance-Owen," I think; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Did the Muslims tell you that joke?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can't remember where I heard it. No, it was certainly not the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I don't think it was the Croats either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, briefly yesterday you talked about the detainees when you were discussing the International Red Cross in Mostar and their monitoring situation; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you said that this subject of the detainees at that time was a hot potato; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Is this the same -- can you -- if you can, is this the same kind of hot potato that is going on right now with the detainees that the United States has in Cuba that they brought from Afghanistan?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, to relevance and just inflammatory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Meek, we come back to all those issues about other matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'll skip that question, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yesterday, Sir Martin, you testified that you felt that Siroki Brijeg had a strong Croat area.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Siroki Brijeg was a very strong Croat area, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you said you felt that way.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a fact. I don't think there were -- I cannot recall any Muslims or Serbs living in Siroki Brijeg. I think it was a totally Croat town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: In another part of your testimony yesterday, you were talking about Mr. Granic, and this was right after you were talking about the hot potato issue with the detainees.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And that you had heard that no one would be released unless they did not return to Bosnia, none of the detainees. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I think I said that I was not aware of precisely -- I think I'd heard something about that but I had no firm knowledge about not being allowed to return to Bosnia, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So in fact, you could not confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. You testified yesterday, Sir Martin, that you had mixed feelings about a situation where the Muslims and the Croats had agreed on the ECMM going to Jablanica. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said -- I think I said it was of interest that both Muslims and Croats expressed enthusiasm for us to return to Jablanica for different reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And I think you used the term that you had mixed feelings about that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps mixed feelings was the wrong phrase. Perhaps I should have said there were mixed motives for Croats and Muslims being -- wishing us to return to Jablanica. No. We were very anxious. We were very anxious to return.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Dobro. But my question would be: Why was it that you had these mixed feelings?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mixed feelings may have been the wrong phrase. We were desperately anxious to get back to Jablanica as quickly as possible. What I think I meant - maybe I didn't phrase it well - was that the reasons for the Croats and Muslims wanting us to go back to Jablanica were different, were mixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: In your testimony in the Kordic case, you testified that in the last six months, the Croats wanted peace. Is that a fact?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly, when I was up at Zenica towards the end of my time, I got the feeling that the Croats wanted to finish the fighting. They were on the defensive. The Bosniaks were making gains. There had been a number of incidents, well, apart from the destruction of the Stari Most. There had also been the massacre at Stupni Do, there had been the serious loss of Vares, which was a very significant strategic loss for the Croats because it meant that the Bosniak army, the ABiH army, could move from Tuzla to Gornji Vakuf without passing through any Croat pockets. So that was very significant. So I got the feeling that they realised that the longer it continued, the more they were going to lose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Would it be a fair statement, Sir Martin, the fact remains that in the last six months before the final peace agreements, the Croats desired peace, strongly desired peace, but it didn't happen for six months because the BH army wouldn't allow it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I started forming these opinions early in the -- at the end of the year, at the end of the year. No Croat general or even political leader said that they wanted peace. It was just my reading of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Very briefly, I believe that you've indicated that you do not recall any reports of looting whatsoever when you were in Mostar. In your statement, you said --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looting, looting from?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Looting, stealing, taking things from people's apartments, taking their cars, taking their valuables, looting.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you just draw my attention to precisely what I said?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sure. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: If I could have the usher's assistance. Page 5 on the English. Just show that to Sir Martin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes. At that time - this is in the summer of 1993 - I do not recall any reports of looting, although I'm quite certain it would have occurred during the expulsions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Meek, that's radically different from what you've put to the witness. So saying "thank you" as if he agreed with you is really a misrepresentation of what the bench hears. Read back what you said and then look at Sir Martin's answer, and I don't need any further comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Judge Clark, is this the question that starts on line 2 of page 69? Okay. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir Martin, I should have said during your time in Bosnia, the three months you were there, but --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: In those three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes. I --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: We know for a fact that many of those who were expelled just walked out with the clothes that they were wearing. So what happened to all their other possessions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: But it's a fact that you said in your report that "I do not recall any reports of looting, although I am sure -- certain that would have occurred during" --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That's all I wanted to ask you, sir. One final question, Sir Martin, and it deals with the Washington Agreement in 1992. Are you aware of the Washington Agreement?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: In March, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: 1994. Pardon me. In that agreement, was the HVO recognised as the lawful military authority in Bosnia-Herzegovina, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was agreed that the HVO and the ABiH would continue in their -- under their present constitution but with a view to combining under a joint command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir Martin, I thank you very much for your patience and your time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any cross-examination, Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Sir Martin. I'm Zelimir Par, and I'm one of the counsel for the accused Vinko Martinovic. I will ask you some questions relevant to your testimony. Yesterday, you could see that we ran into a number of problems when we tried to establish what was your exact position, whether you were here as an expert witness, representative of the International Community, general eyewitness, and so on and so forth. The Chamber ruled that we should treat you as an independent observer. Now, my question is whether you can personally define the position that you are testifying from. That is, can you help us resolve this dilemma? How do you see yourself here? Are you an observer, a general, an eyewitness?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not here -- I'm not here as a general, because I said that throughout my time in Bosnia I was acting in a civilian capacity, but I would say that I am here because of the knowledge and experience I gained during those five and a half years, almost entirely in Mostar, in those four different appointments that I had in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I see. But what I am trying to establish is you were there in the capacity of an observer, that is, a witness qualified to observe certain events. Now, what I'm trying to establish here is whether you are testifying in that capacity or is your testimony the result not only of that particular duty that you held there but of your knowledge in general. I'm not quite sure that I've made myself clear.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope I understand you, but if I could just clarify one point. When I was serving with the EC monitor mission, I would say I was a monitor and an observer, assisting with meetings and doing what we could do. But from then on, it was -- we were actually hands-on engaged in practical work, not just observing but actually doing things.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And so let us perhaps go back. Perhaps you could have a somewhat closer definition of an ECMM. What were the qualifications? What were the criteria that were used in order to designate, to appoint somebody to that post, to become a monitor?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were normally chosen from former majors, lieutenant colonels, as far as the UK is concerned, in the British armed forces. I was actually, in theory, far too old for the task but somehow they accepted me. But if we go on to the qualifications, it was a careful interviewing and vetting to check whether they considered you were a suitable person Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. for this particular task, but initially it was mainly ex-military people because the task -- a military background certainly helped. But then later on, others, former diplomats, lawyers, and others came in. But certainly the military background, because of the nature of the work and the potential -- the potentially dangerous work, a military background was very useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the task of that military observer, was it only to register facts, that is, on the basis of his knowledge to merely record what he had observed and then send on these facts to somebody else who would then judge them or was this monitor's task also to interpret those facts, to make some conclusions, to make some forecasts? What did the task of a monitor mean?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would normally -- we would normally -- as I think I said yesterday, our fundamental task was reporting on political, military, and humanitarian matters, in that order, but we did cover -- carry out a number of other tasks such as chairing meetings, negotiating, helping with humanitarian work and so on. But our reports were not just what we saw or reporting of meetings that we'd had and views that had been expressed to us but nearly always at the end of the report, and particularly end of weekly reports, we would produce an assessment, an assessment of what all this actually meant in the view of the person who was writing the report, and the way things were developing or the possible dangers ahead and so on. So it was interpreting as well as reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So we are still talking about the monitors and their mission. Do they monitor only the conduct of the parties to the conflict or do they also cover the work of other international organisations involved in the conflict, or is it restricted only to the parties to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We'd certainly have meetings with other international organisations. That is where a lot of our information came from. And so there would be discussions not only, for example, in Mostar with the Croats and Bosniaks but also with the military, international military, UNPROFOR, UNHCR, ICRC, and so on, to get as wide as possible pool of knowledge and of views as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that these international organisations were a source of certain information, that they were part of international activity there, but my question is whether your role of monitors also extended to them. Did you report on the activities of UNPROFOR? Did you report perhaps on what the UNHCR was doing, or the Red Cross, and so on and so forth? That is, would you, your role of observer, allow you to also cover their work, to monitor their work and report on their work as well?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes. We -- we -- yes, we would certainly report on, you know, what problems UNHCR were having, what convoys they were running, and UNPROFOR, what difficulties they were facing, what problems they face, and they would seek our advice and we would seek their advice.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I meant something specific in this regard, namely, throughout the war, both sides objected from time to time to UNPROFOR and other organisations involved there. At some point in your testimony, you mentioned that convoys with the humanitarian aid, be it from UNHCR and so forth, were blocked. Are you aware that there were also objections that UNPROFOR vehicles were used to smuggle in weapons or people and so on and so forth, and that many people took that as a pretext for the blockades? Have you had an opportunity to hear anything about it or did you hear anything about it? Did you report about that? Did you hear anything about UNPROFOR or any other international organisation misuse its position in order to cooperate with one of the parties to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: One did hear, one did hear allegations, but I never was given a concrete example to follow up. That never happened. The allegations were always vague and were never substantive enough to enable me or my people to actually pursue a particular line, because you cannot act on just vague allegations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Monitors -- a monitor's job - I'm still there - does it also mean that one makes a political assessment of one of the belligerents? Did you, as a monitor, assess the positions of the Croat side? You heard those positions. And would it be your job to then assess those views and to say, for instance, well, the Croats have no right or the Bosniaks are not right? Would that be part of your task to make political assessments of their ideas?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. One of our tasks must, had to be assessing the information, assessing what we felt was going on, assessing the views of different people and different leaders. This was all part of important information. And if we got our job right, if we did our job well, then back in the capitals they would have solid, concrete facts to work on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So if I understand you well, you followed a specific method. There was a standard model of collecting information, of selecting information, processing it, and then forwarding it. I suppose there is a standard method which you used. It was not left at the discretion of some new head of mission how things would be done. There were certain established rules, certain procedures that you all invariably followed, is that it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, we had -- we -- all the reporting procedures were standardised, but what of course went into the reports varied from monitor to monitor depending on how capable he was, how well he was doing his job, and so on. So different monitors would produce different standards of reporting and different standards of assessments. And so one learnt after awhile that certain individuals' views were significant and important and others, one didn't really bother about them quite so much. So the reporting procedures and so on were all standardised, but how the monitor actually did his job on the ground varied from person to person.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Now, these reports, you observed, you sent your reports, your mission was in full swing, and how was the work of your mission assessed? Were your reports accepted? How was that assessed? Do you get any feedback how they were accepted at some higher level? Did you get any feedback as to how your reports were viewed?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We did not get feedback on a daily basis because people were so busy. But, for example, if one sent in a special report on a particular subject which was significant and which was considered to be a good report, then back would come the message, "Much appreciated, your very good report on so-and-so," and maybe asking a few additional questions which we perhaps might be invited to pursue. So there was feedback, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Now we've covered a certain road, from the manner in which information was gathered, who and how gathered it and who then forwarded it. What I'm interested now is in this feedback. You have just told us that this information reaches a centre or some centre, some hubs, and on the basis of this information, the international commission draws certain moves. Could you please explain it now to me? Where -- what is the final destination for this information, and what is the feedback or, rather, the reverse effect? How does this information or, rather, the feedback, the response, how does it then become a part of a plan or a programme of work or something? Could you perhaps describe more specifically the route that this feedback or reverse information takes?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I say, the majority -- the majority of the messages were going one way. They were going upwards from the coordinating centres to the regional centres, to the headquarters in Zagreb and then off to the EU Presidency and the capitals. Now, I have to say that we did not -- I don't recall getting feedback from capitals. It was -- but we sometimes got feedback from the headquarters of the ECMM in Zagreb. We tended to take the view that no news is good news. And if they had any queries on what we'd said, then they'd come back to us, and as I said, occasionally, thanks and appreciation for a particular report.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I don't mean specifically your work or your reports. I'm, in principal, interested in that information. So that information from the ground must have had some purpose. Somebody, I suppose, would then be invited to act upon -- upon it or, rather, act on the basis of this information, and that again would find its reflection in the events, in the developments on the ground, and that is, I suppose, why it matters whether information is accurate or not, because it would then have again its effect on whatever happens on the ground. Now, my -- what I want to know is the information comes from different places to one centre, and I suppose they are either put -- this information is either put together and then somebody will use it, will determine its purpose, and then at the level of the International Community, somebody's going to use it for something, pursuing some objective or other. Now, what I'm interested in is to know how one uses it, in what way is this information then used?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, then, if I could perhaps give concrete examples. Now, in Bosnia, when I was the head of the coordinating centre in Mostar, I would receive reports from all four of my teams every day. Now, some of that information would be for me to act on. It would require my action. Other, I would be passing on as information up to the regional centre. Some of the information that I passed up to the regional centre would be for them to take action on. Other would be information which they would be forwarding on to the headquarters in Zagreb. And as I say, the final product at the end of the day was the coordinated reports sent from the headquarters in Zagreb to the capitals, giving them a daily snapshot of the whole situation throughout the former Yugoslavia, political, military, and humanitarian in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Why am I insisting upon all this? Perhaps you are aware of that. In Bosnia, a general attitude toward ECMMs was that as of the moment they turned up in Bosnia, all those who could see themselves as victims or did not -- wanted this to disappear, they were all very happy to see those representatives of the international organisation because there would be somebody coming there, seeing what was going on, report it, and then the problem would be resolved. However, very many people were very disenchanted with this mission because the results were either too late or never happened. So my question is: Why is it -- are you aware of this feeling, which is, I should say, a popular feeling there, that more was expected from international organisations, and international organisations and especially the ECMMs somehow fell short of these expectations?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all I can say is that I'm sorry to hear that. I did have views such as like you have expressed to me from time to time, but I must stress again that the ECMM was, as its name implies, was a monitoring organisation. It was not delivering food like UNHCR. It wasn't providing military like UNPROFOR. It wasn't providing the ICRC. It was fundamentally a monitoring organisation to provide, eventually, the foreign offices of the various capitals with information that they needed. As I said, this was a very delicate period. We'd moved on from the Vance-Owen Plan. We were moving into the Invincible talks, the EU action plan, the contract group plan, and so on. These were fast moving days, and it was essential that capitals had a very clear idea of what was happening on the ground. So I know that people may have expected more from the ECMM than the ECMM could deliver, but at least capitals were getting the information which politicians needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: All this was one aspect of the whole matter, that is, you provide some, so to say, inside information, that is, Bosnian information, and send this information on to outside centres. Was it a part of your task to also transmit and implement certain views, certain positions of the International Community in Bosnia? Was a part of your task in Bosnia to try and exercise some influence on the people that you communicated with them by transmitting to them certain views, certain positions of the International Community?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, certainly. And also, as I think I maybe mentioned yesterday, we did also -- the monitors did also take a -- played a part in arranging meetings, negotiating and so on between the different factions, and this was a very important part, to bring -- try and bring the sides together and, where possible, arrange meetings. This was part of the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And perhaps we could now start with those meetings. If I understand you properly, you leave off on a mission. First you have some very general information, then less general about the political, military, humanitarian situation on the ground in the area that you're being sent to. That is part of those briefings. Then you also hear what the International Community thinks about all these issues and the directions in which you should act and what it is that you should focus on. If I am wrong, you will correct me. Now, my question is: During the -- after you had been briefing, after you were about to set off on your mission, do you already have, if I may put it that way, do you already have the special glasses on through which you look at the situation at the mission, glasses provided to you by the International Community? Is it that you already know what you have to concentrate on and what it is you are to do once on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- I think members of the ECMM monitor mission were given a wide degree of latitude, and I think it depended on the calibre and the quality of the various monitors to decide, he might be invited by his superior headquarters to find out, and I often was, "Please could you find out and produce a special report on a particular subject?" But otherwise, we had very much a free hand, and it was up to us to decide what we considered to be important and what we wanted to pursue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: All these questions, Sir Martin, have to do with what I am -- with the position of the defence, namely, we think that the conclusions and these considerations, these analyses, what you gave us during your testimony about the causes for the conflict in Mostar, different relationship, who intended to do what, who picked up which idea, and so on and so forth, so the position of the Defence is that what you testified about is a simplified story about Mostar, seen and experienced to that particular pair of glasses made by the International Community in pursuit of its own political objectives, and where this complex picture was simplified making one party guilty and the other one with its hands completely clean. So that is our position. That is not a question, that is the reason behind all these questions that I asked you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I realise and I appreciate counsel just Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. saying that was not a question, however, I think it is unfair to this witness. This witness had something like five and-a-half years of experience on the ground in Mostar and Zenica. He is probably -- well, it's not for me to say, but an extremely knowledgeable witness about this. To suggest that he has presented a simplified story, I would suggest -- at the same time, the Defence has objected to him talking about anything else that he has learned and confirmed anytime after the first few months of 1994 is unfair to the witness, and his base of information and the basis on which he has said the things that he says.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm also very happy to respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Par, it just seems to me that you are not asking a question but make quite a long statement, which is not allowed. You have to bear in mind that. We understand that you have the different views, you know, compared with the views expressed by this witness, but that's not the right place to state your views.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm very happy to give a response though.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your permission. Mr. President, in this way, I presented the position of the Defence precisely in order to be fair and correct to the witness here, Sir Martin. In other words, there is nothing behind this question, but I am stating our position as it is, and I am trying to test some of the evidence that the witness has given against this. I was in no way trying to diminish the authority of this witness. On the contrary, I believe this is a witness with whom one can carry on this discussion in which two different positions are confronted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So my real question was going to be: Is this way in which you, Sir Martin, presented your views based on what you -- you were prepared to do and was it that he was staying within the framework of what was -- what he was asked to do, and that was then the relevant framework within which he operated?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think if I can respond to that by saying that I think the thrust of your question is by the use of your word "glasses," looking through things from a particular viewpoint and being -- operating to someone's instructions. I think it's in this file somewhere. I seem to remember saying - I think it may have been to Prlic at one stage - that if I was receiving instructions from my own government back in England, I would pack my bags and go back the next day. We were not under political control, absolutely not. It is entirely up to the monitors to report and to present their views. If someone was consistently getting it wrong, then he'd be chucked out. But there was absolutely no pressure brought to bear on monitors as to what they should say and what they shouldn't say. I hope -- I hope that answers the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Can I just say something? Sir Martin, I think that Mr. Par has asked you a very valid question, and he's expressed it as a sort of statement in that the position that he is in, if I understand it correctly, as Defence counsel for Mr. Martinovic, is that you as a senior ECMM monitor had your view of the goings-on, if I can call it that, in the Mostar region predetermined by the politics of the EU, and because of that, you found one side in the wrong and the other side in the right. I think that's what Mr. Par is saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if I can perhaps answer that by saying that I don't think it was the EU that would be providing the policy because, as you probably know, the different members of the EU had very different views on the whole problem in Bosnia. So I don't think there was a really united view coming down. And so, as I say, we were, I believe, totally impartial and certainly not under any form of political direction either nationally or from the ECMM. We were treated as adults, and we were judged by our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I absolutely understand you. My intention was not to allude to any kind of political pressures. I was referring to you as a person, as an individual. You may have had a bias. You come in biased simply because you come equipped with a certain amount of information. So the pair of glasses that I was referring to was a pair of glasses that filters your individual vision. In other words, when you arrived in Bosnia, did you arrive with a particular -- with any particular bias? But what you have told me in your response was you did your best to, a reasonable and a responsible person, to observe things as best you could.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that I confess that when I arrived in Bosnia, I was very ignorant of the situation. Bosnia, at that time, for the people who are thousands of miles away, was a very complex business. I used to read the newspapers, but of course that only gave one hundredth of the story. So I came to Bosnia with a totally, I can assure you, a totally open mind. My views were formed as the weeks and months and years went by.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Right. One of the questions I was going to put to you was whether your views today or the ones presented in your evidence, the same ones that you held then or have they been supplemented by an amount of additional information which you have somehow gathered since. So if we go back to Mostar, are your views about everything that went on there the same as they were in 1993 or have your views undergone a certain kind of evolution since that time?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mostar is certainly a very different place from when I first knew it in 1993 when I left it in 1998, but some of the underlying problems which we've been talking about in the last 48 hours still exist. There's still the wish by many for a third entity, Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. There's still the wish for Mostar to be the capital. There is still the fear of Islamic fundamentalism and so on. A lot of these things, the situation is much, much better, but some of these underlying problems still exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: The specific background of this question were the documents. When you -- when you were given a document, say, by Mr. Scott and it is a report from 1993, and he said -- the question to you is: "Sir Martin, do you still stand by everything that is contained in these reports?" you say, "Yes." My question to you was when you refer to these reports of 1993 and you say that that is so, is that with the hindsight of what you know now or was that -- is that something that you also held as your view back in 1993? I guess that is -- because in 1993, perhaps, it's easier to say that this is fine, but back in 1993, did you have sufficient information to be able to corroborate or confirm this?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think when I was being asked by Mr. Scott to confirm things, I say -- I think I've been saying yes, that is my report and those were my views expressed in that, and I have no reason to change the views of what happened in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I think I understood you now. So I think that we have laid out the foundation sufficiently. We know now where your positions come from. Now we may -- we can go into various specific areas where our views may differ. You will understand that. One of the theories that seemed to be underlying some of your evidence was to portray the opposing sides, the Croatian and the Bosnian Muslim side, according to this theory, the Bosniak Muslims advocated a multi-ethnic community and the Croats opposed it. Is that one of the theories or one of the statements that you or positions that you laid out for us and that you consider one of the causes of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly this is the problem or one of the key problems that we faced in Mostar. Was it going to be a multi-ethnic city or was it going to be a divided city or was it going to be a Croat city? This was a fundamental problem that we faced year after year after year.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So this problem of the division of Mostar is actually the story that extends to all of Bosnia, and so if blown up, it concerns all of Bosnia, is it -- is Bosnia going to be divided or not, partitioned or not? So the Mostar problem is really the same problem in a kernel, because in Bosnia some wanted a division of Bosnia and some wanted something else. The same story really can be taken down and be also seen as the story in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree. And people used to say, and I would agree with it, that Mostar in many ways was a microcosm of Bosnia, particularly in view of its multi-ethnic nature which I described yesterday before the fighting, but we now already have Republika Srpska, and so I wouldn't like to -- to guess what the future holds, but certainly I would have very much liked to have seen a unified Bosnia as it was before the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: If we agree that this is a problem that was sort of -- that trickled down from the larger to smaller, although the microcosm to microcosm, maybe we should focus on this issue, the main issue, that is, the division of Bosnia itself rather than Mostar. And this is perhaps in Mostar a slightly simplified story because Serbs are missing from the picture as is the International Community.
