So let me ask you this: Sir Martin, in -- if in the evidence you provided on Mostar you presented the two sides, the Croat and the Bosniak, do you find it necessary, if we were to look for the real causes of war in Mostar, that we should have included the Serbs, and the Serb aggression in Mostar, the Vance-Owen Plan as all the elements that led up to the conflict of the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mentioned yesterday that I did not consider -- I personally do not consider the war in Bosnia to be a civil war, because it was started off by Serbian aggression. Milosevic and then the paramilitaries, Zeljko Raznjatovic and so on, Bijeljina, and then the JNA, and then within a months 70 per cent of the country was in Serb hands. So I agree there were problems, but if you look, that's why -- if we separate how the fighting started in Bosna with why the Croats and the Muslims started fighting each other. That's what I was trying to do yesterday, and I said that I believed it was a problem of territory, and it may well have been a misreading by the Croats of the Vance-Owen Plan provinces, which I believe maybe the Croats assumed were Croat provinces, whereas that was certainly not the intention. I think then it became a problem of territory and then the shooting started.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I agree with you. That is precisely why I am trying to agree with you on that. There were additional factors involved such as the Serbs and the Vance-Owen Plan which, intentionally or not, did increase the tensions, and that was the consequence of information sent by various international organisations to their capitals, and this came back as the Vance-Owen Plan. My question to you is whether you can agree with me on this: that it is not so simple who was to blame for the 9th of May and the start of conflict, that there are many factors involved, some of which are actually -- do not actually come from the two banks of the Neretva River, and you cannot say in a simplified way that Croats, let's say, for instance, are the bad guys here.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you to an extent. And of course the shooting -- the fighting didn't actually start initially in Mostar. It spread to Mostar. But once it started in Mostar, then I am clearly of the opinion that the HVO had made careful plans. I cited the case yesterday of the -- all the detainees, which required careful planning. So I think that -- I don't think it just erupted. I think there must have been careful planning, because you can't do something that -- I'm sorry. I'm going too fast. This requires a lot of planning, a lot of logistics, and so I am certainly of the view that the fighting was pre-planned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid, Sir Martin, that we're -- our time is up. It is 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your permission, I would continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, I am sorry that we have to keep you for another day. We appreciate your cooperation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's fine. That's fine, Mr. President, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, will you please bring the witness out of the room first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Before you leave, could I just say that in the four months that we've been hearing this case, the exchange between Mr. Par and you, Sir Martin, was the most interesting evidence I've heard, and I hope it continues tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, because of the logistic arrangements, we will resume our sitting tomorrow afternoon at 4.00, at 4.00. So we will rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 24th day of January, 2002, at 4.00 p.m. 24 25
